'''Christine Marie Janis''' is a British–American [[palaeontologist]] whose work focuses on mammalian evolution. She is Professor Emerita of Biology at [[Brown University]] and Honorary Professor in the School of Earth Sciences at the [[University of Bristol]].<ref name="JanisBristol">{{cite web|url=http://www.bris.ac.uk/earthsciences/people/christine-m-janis/index.html|title=Professor Christine Janis - School of Earth Sciences|first=University of|last=Bristol|website=www.bris.ac.uk}}</ref> Her research examines the evolution of mammalian diet and locomotion, particularly in relation to climatic and environmental change during the [[Cenozoic]].

Janis's research has addressed mammalian herbivory, limb biomechanics, and locomotor evolution, with a focus on [[ungulate]]s, [[carnivora]]ns, and [[Macropodoidea|macropodoid marsupials]] (kangaroos). She has received several professional honors, including the George Gaylord Simpson Prize and the [[Romer-Simpson Medal]]. She is an elected Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].

== Early life and education ==
Janis earned a bachelor's degree in Natural Sciences (Zoology) from the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1973, and a PhD in Organismal Biology (Vertebrate Paleontology) from [[Harvard University]] in 1979.<ref name="BrownJanis">{{cite web |title=Janis, Christine |url=https://vivo.brown.edu/display/cjanis |website=Brown University}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
Janis joined [[Brown University]] in 1983, where she served as assistant professor, associate professor, and professor of biology until her retirement in 2016, when she was appointed Professor Emerita.<ref name="BrownJanis" />

She was a visiting professor at the [[University of Chicago]] from 1994 to 1996, and held Benjamin Meaker Fellowships at the [[University of Bristol]] in 2001 and 2008. Since 2015 she has been Honorary Professor in the School of Earth Sciences at the University of Bristol.<ref>{{cite web |title=Professor Christine Janis |url=https://www.bristol.ac.uk/people/person/Christine-Janis-450fb945-9d7d-4004-a540-2524be359b3e/ |publisher=University of Bristol}}</ref> She has also served as an honorary research associate at the [[Field Museum of Natural History]] in Chicago.<ref>{{cite web |title=Honorary Appointments |url=https://www.fieldmuseum.org/page/about/honorary-appointments |website=Field Museum}}</ref>

Since 2019, Janis has been a member of the advisory board of the NOW (New and Old Worlds) Database of Fossil Mammals, a global resource for documenting Cenozoic mammalian occurrences and supporting macroevolutionary and palaeoecological research.<ref>{{cite web |title=NOW - Fossil Mammal Database - Advisory Board |url=https://nowdatabase.org/now/board/ |website=Nowdatabase.org}}</ref>

== Scientific contributions ==
Janis's research examines the evolution of [[Cenozoic]] mammals, with particular attention to relationships between [[morphology (biology)|morphology]], [[Behavior|behaviour]], and environmental change. Her work integrates [[fossil]] evidence with functional and [[Biomechanics|biomechanical]] analyses to reconstruct [[Diet (nutrition)|diet]], [[Animal locomotion|locomotion]], and ecological adaptation in both living and extinct mammals. Much of her research focuses on [[Ungulata|ungulates]], [[carnivora]]ns, and [[Macropodidae|macropodoid marsupials]] (kangaroos).

Janis's first publication addressed competition between [[horse]]s and [[Ruminantia|ruminant]] [[Artiodactyla|artiodactyls]],<ref>{{cite journal|last=Janis|first=Christine M.|year=1976|title=The evolutionary strategy of the Equidae and the origins of rumen and cecal digestion|journal=Evolution|volume=30|issue=4|pages=757–774|doi=10.1111/j.1558-5646.1976.tb00957.x |pmid=28563331 |bibcode=1976Evolu..30..757J }}</ref> a topic she continued to investigate later in her career and revisited in recent work on the drivers of late Cenozoic [[Equidae|equid]] evolution.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janis |first1=C. M. |last2=Brown |first2=S. |last3=Benton |first3=M. J. |last4=Singh |first4=S. |last5=Silvestro |first5=D. |year=2024 |title=Drivers of late Cenozoic equid evolution: The Bull of the Recent |journal=Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, SVP Program and Abstract Book |pages=283–284}}</ref>

She has contributed to research on mammalian [[herbivory]] through analyses of [[dental morphology]] and [[Tooth wear|wear]], particularly in relation to the evolution of [[Hypsodonty|hypsodont]] (high-crowned) cheek teeth. This work includes quantitative studies of dental traits in living ungulates and examinations of the relationships between tooth form, feeding ecology, [[Paleoenvironment|palaeoenvironmental]] reconstruction,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janis |first1=Christine M. |last2=Fortelius |first2=Mikael |title=On the Means Whereby Mammals Achieve Increased Functional Durability of Their Dentitions, with Special Reference to Limiting Factors |journal=Biological Reviews |date=1988 |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=197–230 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-185X.1988.tb00630.x |pmid=3042033 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1469-185X.1988.tb00630.x |language=en |issn=1469-185X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and adaptive responses to increasingly abrasive diets.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Damuth |first1=John |last2=Janis |first2=Christine M. |title=On the relationship between hypsodonty and feeding ecology in ungulate mammals, and its utility in palaeoecology |journal=Biological Reviews |date=2011 |volume=86 |issue=3 |pages=733–758 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-185X.2011.00176.x |pmid=21418504 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1469-185X.2011.00176.x |language=en |issn=1469-185X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Janis has also conducted research on ruminant artiodactyl [[systematics]]<ref>Janis, C.M., and K.M. Scott (1987). The interrelationships of higher ruminant families, with special emphasis on the members of the Cervoidea. American Museum Novitates 2893:1-85</ref> and on patterns of Cenozoic mammalian evolution in relation to [[climate change]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janis |first1=C. M. |last2=Damuth |first2=J. |last3=Theodor |first3=J. M. |title=Miocene ungulates and terrestrial primary productivity: where have all the browsers gone? |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=5 July 2000 |volume=97 |issue=14 |pages=7899–7904 |doi=10.1073/pnas.97.14.7899 |doi-access=free |pmid=10884422 |pmc=16642 |bibcode=2000PNAS...97.7899J |issn=0027-8424}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Figueirido|first1=B.|last2=Janis|first2=C.M.|last3=Pérez-Claros|first3=J.A.|title=Cenozoic climate change influences mammalian evolutionary dynamics|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=2011|volume=109|issue=3|pages=722–727|doi=10.1073/pnas.1110246108 |doi-access=free |pmid=22203974 |pmc=3271923 }}</ref> Her work has contributed to broader analyses of how long-term environmental change is associated with mammalian diversity and ecological specialisation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Over 65 million years, North American mammal evolution has tracked with climate change |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/571665 |website=EurekAlert}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Fossil dogs evolved alongside climate change |url=https://phys.org/news/2015-08-fossil-dogs-evolved-climate.html |website=Phys.org}}</ref>

From the 1990s onward, Janis published extensively on mammalian locomotion and limb biomechanics, demonstrating how limb proportions, joint morphology, and scaling relationships can be used to infer locomotor behaviour in extinct mammals.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Figueirido |first1=Borja |last2=Janis |first2=Christine M. |title=The predatory behaviour of the thylacine: Tasmanian tiger or marsupial wolf? |journal=Biology Letters |date=23 December 2011 |volume=7 |issue=6 |pages=937–940 |doi=10.1098/rsbl.2011.0364 |pmid=21543392 |pmc=3210661 |bibcode=2011BiLet...7..937F |issn=1744-957X}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=B. |last2=Janis |first2=C.M. |title=Hop, walk or bound? Limb proportions in kangaroos and the probable locomotion of the extinct genus ''Protemnodon'' |journal=Journal of Mammalian Evolution |date=2024 |volume=31 |issue=2 |article-number=26 |doi=10.1007/s10914-024-09725-4|doi-access=free }}</ref> This research has provided a functional framework for interpreting [[Postcranial skeleton|postcranial]] fossil material across a range of mammalian groups.

Her publications also include studies of the predatory behaviour of marsupial carnivores, incorporating biomechanical and functional analyses that have been reported in popular science media.<ref>{{cite news |title=Extinct marsupial lion was no killer cat |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/marsupial-saber-tooth-was-no-killer-cat-180975442/ |work=Smithsonian Magazine}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=How marsupial predators killed their prey |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-13270381 |work=BBC News}}</ref>

In more recent research, Janis has examined the evolution of [[horse]] [[Animal locomotion|locomotion]], particularly hypotheses concerning the evolution of a single functional [[toe]] in modern horses.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janis |first1=Christine M. |last2=Bernor |first2=R. L. |year=2019 |title=The evolution of equid monodactyly: A review including a new hypothesis |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution |volume=7 |article-number=119 |doi=10.3389/fevo.2019.00119 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019FrEEv...7..119J |hdl=1983/ede09e37-96f7-4baf-aec5-1bb7766a04e7 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vincelette |first1=A. R. |last2=Renders |first2=E. |last3=Scott |first3=K. M. |last4=Falkingham |first4=P. L. |last5=Janis |first5=Christine M. |year=2023 |title=Hipparion tracks and horses' toes: the evolution of the equid single hoof |journal=Royal Society Open Science |volume=10 |issue=3 |article-number=230358 |doi=10.1098/rsos.230358  |doi-access=free|pmid=37351494 |bibcode=2023RSOS...1030358V }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Why horses evolved a single toe |url=https://phys.org/news/2019-04-toe-horse-legs-evolved.html |website=Phys.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=New scientific evidence overturns earlier theory on horse hoof evolution |url=https://www.horseandrideruk.com/news/new-scientific-evidence-overthrows-earlier-theory-on-horse-hoof-evolution/ |website=Horse & Rider UK |date=26 June 2023 }}</ref> She has also contributed to research on kangaroo locomotion, proposing that extinct short-faced giant kangaroos ([[Sthenurinae|sthenurines]]) used bipedal walking rather than hopping. This interpretation was later supported by fossil [[trackway]] evidence.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janis |first1=Christine M. |last2=Buttrill |first2=K. |last3=Figueirido |first3=B. |year=2014 |title=Locomotion in extinct giant kangaroos: were sthenurines hop-less monsters? |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=9 |issue=10 |article-number=e109888 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0109888 |doi-access=free |pmid=25333823 |pmc=4198187 |bibcode=2014PLoSO...9j9888J }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Extinct giant kangaroos didn't hop – they walked |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg22429914-600-extinct-giant-kangaroos-didnt-hop-they-walked/ |work=New Scientist}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Janis |first1=Christine |editor-first1=Michael |editor-first2=Penny |editor-last1=Lund |editor-last2=Orbell |title=Giant kangaroos were more likely to walk than hop |url=https://theconversation.com/giant-kangaroos-were-more-likely-to-walk-than-hop-32837 |website=The Conversation |date=15 October 2014 |doi=10.64628/AA.g6rs7jssv |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Beyond mammals, Janis has published on the [[Paleobiology|palaeobiology]] of other fossil [[vertebrate]]s, including early vertebrates, early [[Tetrapoda|tetrapods]], [[dinosaur]]s, [[Mesozoic]] mammals, and the timing of divergence among [[Placentalia|placental mammal]] lineages.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Salleh |first1=Anna |title=Antacid armour key to tetrapod survival |url=https://www.abc.net.au/science/articles/2012/04/25/3488040.htm |website=ABC Science |language=en-AU |date=25 April 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Mammals Became More Terrestrial Towards End of Cretaceous Period, Study Shows |url=https://www.sci.news/paleontology/cretaceous-terrestrial-mammals-13793.html |website=Sci.News |date=2 April 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Dinosaurs and the rise of mammals |url=https://www.siliconrepublic.com/innovation/dinosaurs-mammal-ancestors-palaeontology-fossils |website=Silicon Republic}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
* George Gaylord Simpson Prize, [[Yale University]] (1985)<ref>{{cite web |title=George Gaylord Simpson Prize {{!}} Yale Peabody Museum |url=https://peabody.yale.edu/explore/awards-prizes/george-gaylord-simpson-prize |website=Yale.edu |language=en}}</ref>
* Fellow, [[The Paleontological Society]] (2007)<ref>{{cite web |title=Fellows of the Paleontological Society |url=https://www.paleosoc.org/fellows-of-the-paleontological-society |website=Paleontological Society}}</ref>
* Elizabeth Leduc Award, Brown University (2008)<ref>{{cite web |title=Faculty Teaching Award |url=https://dof.brown.edu/resources/teaching/faculty-teaching-award |website=Brown University |language=en}}</ref>
* Honorary Member, [[Society of Vertebrate Paleontology]] (2019)<ref>{{cite web |title=Roster of Honorary Members |url=https://vertpaleo.org/roster-of-honorary-members/ |website=Society of Vertebrate Paleontology}}</ref>
* Elected member, [[Linnean Society of London]] (2022)
* [[Romer-Simpson Medal]], [[Society of Vertebrate Paleontology]] (2024)<ref>{{cite web |title=Award Winners and Grant Recipients |url=https://vertpaleo.org/past-award-winners-and-grant-recipients/ |website=Society of Vertebrate Paleontology}}</ref>
* Elected member, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2025)<ref>{{cite web |title=Christine Marie Janis |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/christine-marie-janis |website=American Academy of Arts and Sciences |language=en |date=21 October 2025}}</ref>

== Books ==
Janis has authored and edited several widely used textbooks and edited volumes on vertebrate evolution and mammalian palaeontology. These include seven editions of ''Vertebrate Life'' (1998–2023),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rubega |first1=Margaret |title=Vertebrate Life. F. Harvey Pough, Christine M. Janis, John B. Heiser |journal=The Quarterly Review of Biology |date=December 1999 |volume=74 |issue=4 |pages=478–479 |doi=10.1086/394168 |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/394168 |issn=0033-5770|url-access=subscription }}</ref> with Harvey Pough as senior author, and two volumes of the reference work ''Evolution of Tertiary Mammals of North America'' (1998,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Novacek |first1=Michael |title=Evolution of Tertiary Mammals of North America. Volume 1: Terrestrial Carnivores, Ungulates, and Ungulatelike Mammals. Christine M. Janis, Kathleen M. Scott, Louis L. Jacobs |journal=The Quarterly Review of Biology |date=September 2000 |volume=75 |issue=3 |pages=309–310 |doi=10.1086/393518 |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/393518 |issn=0033-5770|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 2008),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Naish |first1=Darren |title=C. M. Janis, G. F. Gunnell & M. D. Uhen (eds) 2008. Evolution of Tertiary Mammals of North America. Volume 2: Small Mammals, Xenarthrans, and Marine Mammals|journal=Geological Magazine |date=March 2010 |volume=147 |issue=2 |page=317 |doi=10.1017/S001675680900630X |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/geological-magazine/article/abs/c-m-janis-g-f-gunnell-m-d-uhen-eds-2008-evolution-of-tertiary-mammals-of-north-america-volume-2-small-mammals-xenarthrans-and-marine-mammals-viii-795-pp-cambridge-new-york-melbourne-cambridge-university-press-price-15000-hard-covers-isbn-9780-521-78117-6/17D241A9D33B00E3DA9384BA9AF13637 |language=en |issn=1469-5081|url-access=subscription }}</ref> for which she served as senior editor.

== Personal life ==
In addition to her research on fossil horses, Janis has been a life-long equestrian. She was married to palaeontologist [[Jack Sepkoski]] (1948–1999).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Yoon |first1=Carol Kaesuk |title=J. John Sepkoski Jr., 50, Dies; Changed Field of Paleontology |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/06/us/j-john-sepkoski-jr-50-dies-changed-field-of-paleontology.html |publisher=NY Times |language=en}}</ref>

== Public engagement ==
Janis has contributed to public understanding of science through radio and television appearances, including participation in [[BBC Radio 4]]'s ''[[In Our Time (radio series)|In Our Time]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=BBC Audio {{!}} In Our Time {{!}} The Evolution of Horses |url=https://www.bbc.com/audio/play/m000fp9y |website=Bbc.com}}</ref> She served as a scientific advisor for the Netflix documentary series ''[[Life on Our Planet]]'' (2023), and has provided extensive advisory input for a forthcoming BBC television series on evolution.<ref>{{cite web |title=BBC reveal new Chris Packham-fronted series Evolution |url=https://virginradio.co.uk/entertainment/151083/bbc-reveal-new-chris-packham-fronted-series-evolution |website=Virgin Radio |date=10 July 2024 }}</ref>
